sourceBindings.text: Soil pH is a measure of acidity or alkalinity of a soil-water system. It influences nutrient chemical forms, soil organisms and root conditions, so it helps interpret crop health. It does not identify the cause of every yellow or stunted plant. Water, salinity, root injury, disease and nutrient supply remain possible explanations.

The source compares nutrients to treasure behind a locked door and pH to a key. Use it to remember that a soil can contain an element while its available form or uptake is restricted. The analogy is not literal: pH does not turn all uptake completely on or off. We will first understand and interpret a measured result; the later measurement and amendment steps use equipment, crop targets and laboratory guidance before recommending a treatment.

sourceBindings.text: On the familiar teaching scale, pH below 7.0 is acidic, 7.0 is neutral, and above 7.0 is alkaline under ordinary classroom conditions. For example 5.0 is acidic, 8.0 is alkaline and 6.8 is slightly acidic rather than exactly neutral. The 0–14 diagram is a convenient common teaching range, not a claim that every possible solution must be inside it.

A low number means greater hydrogen-ion activity than a higher number under comparable measurement conditions. A pH result is not by itself a lime, sulfur or fertilizer rate; soil buffering, crop needs and calibrated testing matter.

sourceBindings.text: The pH number is logarithmic: a decrease of one whole pH unit corresponds to about ten times greater hydrogen-ion activity. Thus pH 5.0 has ten times the hydrogen-ion activity of pH 6.0; pH 5.0 has one hundred times that of pH 7.0; and pH 4.5 has ten times that of pH 5.5. Name which sample is lower before giving the factor so the direction cannot be reversed.

This factor describes hydrogen-ion activity, not a tenfold lime dose, a tenfold danger, or ten times less crop yield. If using the source's earthquake analogy, a one-unit magnitude difference corresponds roughly to tenfold measured wave amplitude, while released energy differs by about 32-fold; saying only 'ten times stronger' is misleading. The direct pH examples are sufficient without the analogy.

sourceBindings.text: pH can change solubility and reactions of nutrient forms, root function and microbial processes. This helps explain how a test can detect an element while plants still fail to obtain enough of it. 'Locked up' is a useful shorthand for restricted availability, not absolute absence or a universal block on absorption.

Many common crops, including maize and soybean, often perform well in a mildly acidic to near-neutral range such as pH 6.0–7.0, but crop and soil targets vary. Some crops prefer other ranges. The relevant target comes from the crop, soil test, region and local agronomic guidance, not from memorizing one number for all agriculture.

sourceBindings.text: In sufficiently acid mineral soils, P can react with Al and Fe and become less available; Ca and Mg supply or uptake can also be limiting. Soluble aluminum (Al) and manganese (Mn) can increase, and at sufficiently high concentrations may injure roots or plants. Soil biology, including some nitrogen-fixing associations in legumes, can also be less effective under unfavourable acidity.

The source shorthand 'below pH 6' is not a toxicity test. Al and Mn risk depends on how acid the soil actually is and on soil type, element concentration, crop and other conditions; risk often rises more clearly below about pH 5.5. A pH 5.0 scenario warrants investigation, not an automatic statement that toxicity is present or that every phosphate ion is unavailable.

sourceBindings.text: At high pH, iron (Fe), manganese (Mn) and zinc (Zn) can be less available to plants; P may also be less available where it reacts with calcium. Some crops can show chlorosis when Fe uptake is limited even if soil contains Fe. High pH is one possible reason an iron supplement appears not to solve yellowing, but leaf colour or treatment history alone does not prove the cause.

Confirm the measured pH using an appropriate method, identify the crop and tissue age, inspect roots and water management, and consider crop-appropriate soil and tissue results. A yellow leaf might also reflect other nutrient, disease or root problems. Choose an amendment type and rate only after later diagnostic steps and local recommendations.

Some crops can show chlorosis when Fe uptake is limited even if soil contains Fe. High pH is one possible reason an iron supplement appears not to solve yellowing, but leaf colour or treatment history alone does not prove the cause.

Confirm the measured pH using an appropriate method, identify the crop and tissue age, inspect roots and water management, and consider crop-appropriate soil and tissue results. A yellow leaf might also reflect other nutrient, disease or root problems. Choose an amendment type and rate only after later diagnostic steps and local recommendations.

sourceBindings.text: Start near pH 6–7: many nutrients are often reasonably available for many field crops, but no bar can promise uptake. Move to an acidic example at pH 5: phosphorus availability may be restricted and soluble aluminum risk may be higher. Move to an alkaline example at pH 8: iron availability may be lower. For each, say 'may' and name what a field or laboratory check would add.

The axis uses regular pH intervals and correct element names. Read the trends qualitatively with crop and soil context. Neither a bar’s width nor a general diagram is a measured concentration or a diagnosis of toxicity.

sourceBindings.text: pH interpretation builds on the N, P and K functions and fertilizer-label conventions already taught. It helps explain why a nutrient listed on a fertilizer bag might still be poorly supplied to roots. Next, measure and interpret pH with an appropriate kit and laboratory context before considering crop-specific amendment choices.
